This desynchronization skews their sun-based compass, leading to measurable navigational deviations of up to 15 degrees during homing flights. The findings were derived from GPS data of 3,688 foraging trips by 1,045 birds, though the study notes it is not a controlled experiment and cannot confirm other jet lag symptoms like sleep disruption.

The research suggests that animals with internal clocks moving across longitudes may routinely experience jet lag, offering potential insights for designing bio-inspired autonomous navigation systems and understanding how organisms cope with circadian disruption.

A Science study indicates the Laurentide Ice Sheet began re-expanding roughly 2,000 years ago, an event the researchers interpret as the opening move of the next glaciation. This natural advance was reversed around 1960 due to human-caused climate warming. Researchers used beryllium-10 and radiocarbon dating of buried mosses to reconstruct the ice sheet's history, noting that current warming has eliminated the Barnes Ice Cap's accumulation zone.

Why it matters

The findings show that anthropogenic greenhouse gas emissions interrupted a natural glacial cycle that had been progressing for millennia, altering the trajectory of Earth's climate system.

The findings show that anthropogenic greenhouse gas emissions interrupted a natural glacial cycle that had been progressing for millennia, altering the trajectory of Earth's climate system.

Daily News

Science · Technology

Crows can evaluate visual info twice as fast as mammals

Global · Notable · Catch up

Briefing produced 31 Oct 2026, 3:00 AM NZDT

Researchers found that crows solve a random-dot-motion decision task twice as fast as primates, averaging 235 milliseconds compared to 410–600 milliseconds for monkeys, while maintaining comparable accuracy. Neural recordings from 248 neurons in the crows' NCL showed evidence accumulation similar to primate neocortex activity, despite the birds' distinct brain architecture. The study, limited to two crows, suggests that faster neural processing driven by smaller neuron size and higher body temperature may underlie this speed advantage.

Why it matters

The findings demonstrate that evolution has independently converged on similar decision-making mechanisms in birds and mammals, offering insights into how different brain architectures process visual information efficiently.

Analysts suggest this split could be tied to the diversification benefits of owning multiple chains, which may offset weak performance in one brand. Upcoming quarterly earnings will test whether this portfolio strategy continues to outperform single-brand models.

Cadillac Escalade IQ review: Huge battery, huge range, huge SUV

Global · Useful · Catch up

Briefing produced 30 Oct 2026, 9:21 PM NZDT

Ars Technica reviewed the Cadillac Escalade IQ, a heavy electric SUV with a 200+ kWh battery and a claimed 460-mile EPA range. The vehicle features 680 hp standard, air suspension, and a 55-inch display, weighing 9,046 lb. While it achieves 2.1 miles/kWh efficiency, equivalent to over 70 mpg, it lacks a published 10–80% fast-charge time.

Why it matters

The review highlights the Escalade IQ as a viable alternative to gas-powered models, offering significantly higher efficiency (over 70 mpg equivalent vs. 16 mpg for the V8) and substantial range, despite its heavy weight and premium price.
